Lab 21

A ball in a cup of water

Make a glass of water that sloshes, drag a ball across it to leave ripples, then lift the ball and let gravity drop it in: a splash of rings, lit and rendered so it looks like a photograph. Thirty-two small steps, every one animated.

Start the lab

Rendered in Blender by following the steps in this lab.

Today

We are learning

how three different simulations share one scene: an Ocean modifier that makes a glass of water slosh, Dynamic Paint that lets a ball leave ripples on it, and a Rigid Body that drops the ball in; and how glass, water, light and a camera turn the result into a picture that looks real.

You need Blender 4.2 or newer (this lab was built in 5.2), a mouse with a scroll wheel and a middle button (laptop trackpad? see this fix), and about three lessons. Save your file as Lab21_BallInACup_YourName.blend.

You’ve got it when you can

  • build a glass from a cylinder with Solidify, Bevel and Subdivision, and give it a Glass material with the right IOR
  • make a cylinder of water whose top copies a hidden, animated Ocean plane with a Shrinkwrap
  • set up a Dynamic Paint canvas and brush, and make ripples by dragging the brush while the film plays
  • drop a rigid-body ball into a rigid-body cup, predict how many frames the drop takes, and bake it
  • light glass with a sky, a sun and a soft key light, place a camera by number, and render a still and an .mp4

The plan

Five parts, 32 small steps. Each part ends with a picture of what yours should look like.

  1. Part 1The glass and the tableSteps 1–8
  2. Part 2Water that movesSteps 9–16
  3. Part 3The ball, ripples by handSteps 17–21
  4. Part 4GravitySteps 22–26
  5. Part 5Light, camera, renderSteps 27–32

Three simulations, one glass

Nothing in this scene is animated by hand. The slosh comes from an Ocean modifier on a plane you never see; the water’s top copies it. The ripples come from Dynamic Paint: the water is a canvas, the ball is a brush, and wherever the brush touches, rings spread out and bounce off the glass. The drop comes from a Rigid Body: gravity pulls the ball, the cup stops it, and the water is not in the way at all. Three separate systems that do not know about each other, and it looks like one splash.

Then the look is four materials and three lights, every number given a reason.

Word bank — open this if a word in the steps is new
Modifier
A change applied on top of a mesh without editing it: Solidify, Bevel, Subdivision, Ocean, Shrinkwrap. They run top to bottom in the stack.
Solidify
Gives a surface thickness: a tube becomes a glass with a wall.
Grid Fill
Fills a ring of edges with a lattice of squares instead of one flat face.
Ocean modifier
Turns a plane into a sea. Time is its clock; keyframe it and the waves move.
Shrinkwrap
A modifier that pulls one object’s vertices onto another’s surface. Project along Z: straight up or down only.
Limit
In Shrinkwrap, the furthest a vertex may be from the target and still move.
Keyframe
A saved value at one frame, shown as a yellow box or diamond. Blender fills in the frames between.
Dynamic Paint
One object (the brush) leaves marks on another (the canvas). With Surface Type Waves the marks are ripples.
Damping
How fast the ripples die away: 0 never, 1 at once.
Clamp
The biggest push a brush can give the waves.
Rigid Body
Physics for solid objects. Active ones fall and collide; Passive ones only get collided with.
Collision shape
The simple shape the physics uses instead of the real mesh: Sphere, Box, Convex Hull, Mesh.
Bake
Work out every frame of a simulation once and store it, so scrubbing and rendering are reliable.
IOR
Index of refraction: how much a material bends light. Air 1, water 1.33, glass 1.45.
Transmission
How much light passes through a material. 1 is clear glass; 0 is paint.
Rendered view
The viewport showing lights and materials as the render will (Z › Rendered). Slower.
Rename (F2)
A small box that opens over the viewport for typing the selected object’s name. Every name in this lab goes in here. Not F3, which is Search.
Key light
The main light a picture is built around; a big soft one gives soft shadows.
Cycles / EEVEE
Blender’s two renderers: Cycles traces light slowly and accurately, EEVEE draws fast like a game.

Part 1

The glass and the table

Tools: Add › Mesh › Cylinder, the Add Cylinder panel, Edit Mode, Solidify, Bevel, Subdivision Surface, a Glass material, and a Wave Texture for wood.

Five things, three simulations, one file. Before any of the water moves, the glass has to exist: a cylinder with its lid taken off and a wall given to it by a modifier. Then a table for it to stand on. Every step below is one or two moves with its own animation of the mouse doing them: do the move, look at the drawing, do the next.

How the steps work

Each step has a Where line (which part of the Blender window to look at), a Watch animation of the mouse doing the step (pause it, drag the slider, or use the arrow buttons to go one move at a time), and a Do this list of the same moves as a, b, c. The drawings are simplified, not screenshots: the words, numbers and positions match Blender; colours and spacing may not. A gold outline marks a box you type into; Blender itself keeps it grey. Orange, yellow and green boxes mean something real in Blender: changed, keyed here, keyed elsewhere; you meet them in Step 13.

Two keys that look alike. F2 renames the selected object: a small box opens, you type the name, Enter. F3 is Search, for finding tools. Every name in this lab (Cup, Water, OceanPlane, Ball, Key…) is typed into the F2 box; none of them is a tool.

One dropdown to read twice. The Dynamic Paint panel (Steps 18 and 19) opens on Canvas for every object. The water is a canvas; the ball must be changed to Brush before you click Add. Leave it on Canvas and nothing will ever ripple.

  1. Start fresh and save

    Layout workspace › the File menu at the very top-left.

    Do this:

    1. a
      File › New › General. Click the cube, X then Delete. Keep the camera and the light: both are set up in Part 5.
    2. b
      File › Save As. Find your Lab 21 folder, type Lab21_BallInACup_YourName and click Save Blender File.
    3. c
      From now on press Ctrl+S every few steps. This file ends up running three simulations at once; a save costs you one step, a crash costs a lesson.

    You should now see: an empty grid with a camera and a light, and your file name in the window title.

    Why delete the cube?

    Nothing in this scene is a box. The cup and the water are cylinders, the table is a plane, the ball is a sphere; all four come from the Add menu in the next steps.

  2. A cylinder, sized like a glass

    The viewport’s Add menu, then the Add … panel that opens bottom-left of the viewport (click its title if it is folded).

    Predict first: The panel’s Location Z is the middle of the cylinder. Before you type, where will the bottom land with Depth 1.2 and Z 0.6?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cylinder. A fat 2 m cylinder appears, half under the grid.
    2. b
      Open the Add Cylinder panel. Vertices 48. Radius 0.5. Depth 1.2. Location Z 0.6. Enter after each.
    3. c
      F2: the Rename Active Item box opens. Type Cup, Enter.

    You should now see: a 1 m wide, 1.2 m tall tube standing on the grid, and “Cup” in the Outliner (top right).

    Why Z 0.6, and why 48?

    The panel’s Location is the cylinder’s centre, so Depth 1.2 and Z 0.6 put the bottom exactly on the grid (0.6 − 0.6 = 0). 48 sides instead of 32 keeps the rim round once the glass is see-through: every corner shows in a refraction.

  3. Take the lid off

    The viewport, in Edit Mode.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Mouse over the viewport, Tab for Edit Mode. Press 3 for face select (or click the third of the three little icons in the header).
    2. b
      Click the top face: it turns orange. X then Faces.
    3. c
      Tab back to Object Mode.

    You should now see: the cylinder open at the top, like a tube with a bottom.

    Why only the top?

    A glass is a tube with a floor. The floor stays; the lid goes so the ball can fall in. In Step 10 the same move makes the water, and there the lid is deleted with Only Faces because its rim of edges is needed for a Grid Fill.

  4. Give the glass a wall

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue wrench tab

    Do this:

    1. a
      With the Cup selected, Add Modifier › Generate › Solidify.
    2. b
      Thickness 0.04, Enter. Offset stays at -1: the wall grows inward, so the outside of the glass stays exactly 0.5 m.

    You should now see: a cylinder with a visible rim 4 cm thick, like a real tumbler.

    Why a modifier and not a second cylinder?

    Solidify builds the inner wall and the thick rim from the one mesh, and keeps them matched if you change the cup. A second cylinder would need its own lid removed, its own bevel, and would never quite line up.

  5. Round it and smooth it

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue wrench tab, then the viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add Modifier › Generate › Bevel. Amount 0.02, Segments 2. The rim gets a tiny rounded edge: glass is never knife-sharp.
    2. b
      Add Modifier › Generate › Subdivision Surface. Levels Viewport 2. The stack reads Solidify, Bevel, Subdivision.
    3. c
      Right-click the viewport › Shade Smooth. The faceting disappears.

    You should now see: a smooth tumbler with a soft rim.

    Why in this order?

    Modifiers run top to bottom. Solidify first makes the wall; Bevel rounds the wall’s edges; Subdivision smooths what is left. Bevel after Subdivision would find no edges to round.

  6. Glass

    Properties editor › the red sphere Material tab

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click New. Name box: Glass, Enter.
    2. b
      Roughness 0 (polished). IOR 1.45: how much glass bends light.
    3. c
      Open Transmission and set Weight 1: light goes through.

    You should now see: in the viewport nothing changes yet (Solid shading ignores materials). Rendered, in Step 21, this is glass.

    What is IOR?

    Index of refraction: how much a material slows and bends light. Air 1.0, water 1.33, glass 1.45, diamond 2.42. Transmission 1 lets the light through; IOR decides how it bends on the way in. Try the slider under Step 16.

  7. A table

    Add › Mesh › Plane, then the N sidebar › Item tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Plane. Leave it at the origin: the cup is standing on it.
    2. b
      N for the sidebar. Scale X 3, Y 3, Z 3. A 6 m table.
    3. c
      F2: Table, Enter.

    You should now see: a big square under the cup.

  8. Wood, from a wave

    The Shading workspace tab at the top; its node editor is the bottom half.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Table selected. Click Shading at the top. In the node editor click New; F2 the material Wood.
    2. b
      Shift › A › Texture › Wave Texture. Scale 6, Distortion 5, Detail 4. Shift › A › Converter › Color Ramp.
    3. c
      Wire Wave Fac → Ramp Fac, Ramp Color → Principled Base Color. Click the ramp’s left stop, Hex 7A4A26; right stop, Hex C08A55. Roughness 0.3. Back to Layout.

    You should now see: in the Shading viewport, a plank-grain pattern on the table (press Z › Material Preview in Layout to see it there).

    Where does the grain come from?

    A Wave Texture is stripes. Distortion bends the stripes with noise, Detail adds the fine wobble: that is what wood grain is, bent stripes. The Color Ramp turns the black-and-white stripes into two browns.

End of Part 1. Save. Say what Solidify, Bevel and Subdivision each did to the cup, in order.

Part 2

Water that moves

Tools: a second cylinder, Only Faces, Alt+click, Grid Fill, a hidden plane with an Ocean modifier, keyframes on its Time, Shrinkwrap and a Simple subdivision.

The Word lab’s trick, kept whole: the Ocean modifier only works on a flat plane, so a plane makes the waves and the water copies them. The water is a cylinder whose top is a grid of small squares; a Shrinkwrap modifier pulls that grid onto a hidden, rippling plane. Eight steps, and at the end of them the cup sloshes.

  1. A cylinder of water

    Add › Mesh › Cylinder, then the Add … panel that opens bottom-left of the viewport (click its title if it is folded).

    Predict first: 0.49 − 0.43 and 0.49 + 0.43: where are the bottom and the top of this water?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cylinder. Panel: Vertices 48, Radius 0.45, Depth 0.86, Location Z 0.49.
    2. b
      F2: Water, Enter.

    You should now see: a second, slightly smaller cylinder inside the cup, from 6 cm above the floor to 0.92 m, three-quarters full.

    Why 0.45 and 0.49?

    The cup wall is 0.04 thick, so its inside is radius 0.46; a water radius of 0.45 sits just inside it. Centre 0.49 with depth 0.86 puts the water’s bottom at 0.06 (above the glass floor) and its surface at 0.92: the water line.

  2. A surface made of squares

    The viewport in Edit Mode, then the Face menu in the header.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Water selected. Tab, face mode (3). Click the top face, X, then Only Faces: the lid goes but its ring of edges stays.
    2. b
      Switch to edge mode (2). Alt+click one edge of the rim: the whole rim lights up (48 edges).
    3. c
      Face › Grid Fill. A grid of squares fills the circle. In the panel bottom-left, Span 12 if it is not already. Tab.

    You should now see: the top of the water covered by a neat 12 × 12 lattice of squares bent to the circle.

    Why Grid Fill instead of the lid?

    The lid was one big 48-sided face: one flat sheet. Waves need the surface to be lots of small faces so each one can rise and fall on its own. Grid Fill makes 193 faces; the Subdivision in Step 15 makes 12 000.

  3. The wave machine: a plane

    Add › Mesh › Plane, then the N sidebar › Item tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Plane. Sidebar: Location Z 0.92, the water line.
    2. b
      Scale X 0.6, Y 0.6, Z 0.6: a 1.2 m square, a little wider than the cup.
    3. c
      F2: OceanPlane, Enter.

    You should now see: a square floating at the water line, poking out of the glass on all sides. (It gets hidden in Step 15.)

    A plane? The water is a cylinder.

    The Ocean modifier only works on a plane. The trick from the Word lab: let a hidden plane make the waves, and make the water’s top copy it (Shrinkwrap, Step 14). The plane is the engine; the cylinder is the body.

  4. An ocean, shrunk to a cup

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue wrench tab

    Do this:

    1. a
      OceanPlane selected. Add Modifier › Physics › Ocean. A 50 m sea swallows the scene.
    2. b
      Resolution Viewport 10, Render 10. Spatial Size 3: the sea becomes 3 m across.
    3. c
      Waves › Scale 0.04: 4 cm waves. Choppiness 1.5: peaky, not rounded.

    You should now see: the plane rippled with small waves, the cup standing in a little 3 m sea (the plane’s own 1.2 m square is what the Shrinkwrap will read).

    What do the numbers mean?

    Spatial Size is the metres one tile of ocean covers; the Scale slider on the plane cut it down again. Wave Scale is the height of the waves. Choppiness pulls the peaks together into points: real wind-blown water is choppy. The Word lab used a 200 m Depth and Resolution 14 for a swimming-pool-sized scene; a cup needs a cup-sized sea.

  5. Make time pass

    the Timeline along the bottom of the window, then the Ocean panel in Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue wrench tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Timeline: End 120 (five seconds at 24 frames a second). The current frame box reads 1.
    2. b
      Ocean panel › Time: hover the box, type 1, Enter. Still hovering it, press I. The box turns yellow: a keyframe.
    3. c
      Frame box: 120, Enter. Time 6, Enter, I. Two keys. Drag the blue frame marker: the waves roll.

    You should now see: the Time box yellow on frames 1 and 120, green in between, and the waves moving as you scrub.

    Why key Time at all?

    The Ocean modifier is a photograph of a sea at one moment; Time is the clock. Nothing moves until the clock is animated. One key at each end makes it run from 1 to 6 over 120 frames; a bigger gap means faster waves.

  6. Shrinkwrap: the water copies the ocean

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue wrench tab

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Water (click a wall of it, or Water in the Outliner). Add Modifier › Deform › Shrinkwrap.
    2. b
      Wrap Method Project. Axis Z. Tick Negative and Positive: every vertex looks straight up and down for the target.
    3. c
      Limit 0.3: only vertices within 0.3 m of the target move. Target: click the box, choose OceanPlane.

    You should now see: the top of the water jumps onto the waves. Scrub the timeline: it sloshes. The bottom and the walls stay put.

    Why Project, and why Limit 0.3?

    Nearest Surface Point (the default) would drag the water’s walls sideways onto the plane. Project along Z moves each vertex only up or down. Limit 0.3 is the safety: the top grid is 0 m from the plane and moves; the bottom ring is 0.86 m away and is left alone. Without the limit the whole cylinder would collapse onto the plane.

  7. Dense, smooth, and the engine out of sight

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue wrench tab, then the Outliner (top right).

    Do this:

    1. a
      Water still selected. Add Modifier › Generate › Subdivision Surface. Click Simple. Levels Viewport 3, Render 3.
    2. b
      Right-click the viewport › Shade Smooth.
    3. c
      Outliner › the OceanPlane row: click its eye (hidden in the viewport) and its camera icon (hidden in renders).

    You should now see: the water’s surface glassy and dense; the square plane gone. Scrub: the water still sloshes.

    Why Simple, and does hiding break it?

    Catmull-Clark (the default) would also round the water’s rim and shrink it away from the glass; Simple only cuts each face into smaller ones, which is all the waves need. Hidden objects still work: the Shrinkwrap reads the OceanPlane whether or not you can see it.

  8. Water

    Properties editor › the red sphere Material tab

    Do this:

    1. a
      Water selected. New. Name Water.
    2. b
      Base Color › click the swatch › Hex › DCEEF5: almost white, a breath of blue. Roughness 0.02.
    3. c
      IOR 1.33. Transmission › Weight 1.

    You should now see: nothing new in Solid view; in Rendered view (Step 21) the water is see-through and bends light less than the glass.

    Glass 1.45, water 1.33: does it matter?

    That difference is what makes it look wet. Light bends once going into the glass and again going into the water, so the ball’s outline breaks at the water line. The slider below shows the bend.

    Refraction explorer

    A ray of light meets a surface at 50°. Drag the IOR and watch how far it bends; the stick on the right is seen through the side of the cup.

End of Part 2. Save. Scrub the timeline from 1 to 120 and watch the water slosh. Then explain to the person next to you why the plane is hidden but still working.

Part 3

The ball, and ripples by hand

Tools: Add › Mesh › UV Sphere, a Rubber material, Dynamic Paint (a Canvas on the water, a Brush on the ball), Space to play, G to drag, Z › Rendered.

The second Word lab, inside the cup. Dynamic Paint is Blender’s way of letting one object leave marks on another; with the surface type set to Waves the marks are ripples. The water is the canvas, the ball is the brush, and you make the ripples yourself by dragging the ball while the film plays.

  1. A rubber ball on the water

    Add › Mesh › UV Sphere, then the Add … panel that opens bottom-left of the viewport (click its title if it is folded), then Properties editor › the red sphere Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. Panel: Radius 0.15, Location Z 0.9. A ball sitting half in the water, in the middle of the cup.
    2. b
      Right-click › Shade Smooth. F2: Ball, Enter.
    3. c
      Material tab › New › name Rubber. Base Color Hex F05A28. Roughness 0.4.

    You should now see: an orange ball floating in the middle of the cup, named Ball in the Outliner.

    Why on the water first, not in the air?

    Part 3 makes ripples by dragging the ball across the water while the film plays. Part 4 lifts it up and lets gravity drop it. Dragging a ball that is also falling is a fight you lose, so the two tricks are learned one at a time.

  2. The water becomes a canvas

    Properties editor › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column)

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Water. Physics tab › Dynamic Paint. The Type box says Canvas: leave it. Click Add Canvas.
    2. b
      Surface Type: change Paint to Waves. The canvas takes ripples, not colour.
    3. c
      Open Waves: Damping 0.05. Open Frames: End 120, to match the film.

    You should now see: a Dynamic Paint panel on the Water with Surface Type Waves and a Damping of 0.05. Nothing moves yet: no brush.

    What is a canvas?

    Dynamic Paint has two roles: a canvas is the thing that gets marked, a brush is the thing that marks it. With Surface Type Waves the marks are height, and they spread out as rings, bounce off the edge and fade. Damping is how fast they fade: 0 rings forever, 1 no rings at all. Try the ripple tank below.

    Ripple tank

    Exactly what Dynamic Paint Waves computes: a height for every square, pushed by its neighbours, bouncing off the glass. Click or drag on the water.

  3. The ball becomes a brush

    Properties editor › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column)

    Predict first: If you left Type on Canvas and clicked Add Canvas, what would the ball do to the water?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Ball. Physics tab › Dynamic Paint. The Type box says Canvas again: change it to Brush. Then click Add Brush.
    2. b
      Source: Mesh Volume (the default). Check it: the whole ball counts, not just its centre point.
    3. c
      Open Waves: Clamp 0.06. The hardest push the ball can give the water is 6 cm.

    You should now see: a Dynamic Paint panel on the Ball that says Brush, with a Remove Brush button. Canvas and brush: the pair is complete.

    The dropdown trap

    The Dynamic Paint panel opens on Canvas every time. If you click Add Canvas on the ball, the ball becomes a second canvas and nothing ever ripples. The Type box is the one to read. Clamp stops a fast drag throwing the water out of the cup: without it the splash in Part 4 is a geyser.

  4. Play, and drag the ball

    The viewport, with the film playing.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Mouse over the viewport, Space. The film plays from frame 1; the frame counter top-left runs; the waves slosh.
    2. b
      While it plays, hover the ball, press G and move the mouse. Drag the ball across the water. Rings spread out behind it and bounce off the glass. Click to drop it there.
    3. c
      Space to pause. Shift+← rewinds to frame 1: flat water, the ball where you left it. Play again and drag it somewhere else.

    You should now see: rings that race out from the moving ball, bounce off the wall and fade, on top of the slosh.

    Why only while it plays?

    Dynamic Paint is computed one frame after another: each frame’s water is last frame’s water plus whatever the brush did. Pause the film and the water stops; rewind and it starts flat. Moving the ball while paused does nothing until the next frame is computed.

  5. See it as glass and water

    Properties editor › the camera-back Render tab, then the viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Render tab: tick Raytracing. EEVEE needs it to bend light through glass and water.
    2. b
      Mouse over the viewport, Z › Rendered. The glass turns to glass, the water to water.
    3. c
      Play and drag again: the ripples catch the light. Pause (Space) when you are not watching, Rendered view is slower.

    You should now see: a see-through tumbler with real-looking water in it, on a wooden table, under a dark sky. Not matching? See the cup is not see-through.

    Why is the background black?

    Rendered view shows the World, and the default world is near-black. Step 27 gives it a pale sky; the glass and the water reflect that sky, which is most of what makes them look wet.

End of Part 3. Save. Rewind, play, and drag the ball in a circle: watch the rings behind it cross each other.

Part 4

Gravity

Tools: the sidebar numbers, Rigid Body (Active on the ball, Passive on the cup), Space, and Bake.

Lab 9A’s physics, pointed at the water. The ball goes up into the air and gets a Rigid Body so gravity pulls it; the cup gets a Passive one so it can catch it. The water gets nothing: the ball must pass through it, and the Dynamic Paint brush from Part 3 is what makes the splash when it does.

  1. Lift the ball

    the N sidebar › Item tab

    Predict first: Will a heavier ball reach the water sooner? Decide now, then test it in the widget.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Ball. N for the sidebar. Location X 0.12, Y 0.05, Z 2. Enter after each.
    2. b
      It floats 0.93 m above the water, a little off centre so it does not land dead straight.

    You should now see: the ball hanging in the air above the cup.

    How long will it take to fall?

    Height = 4.9 × t², so t = √(0.93 ÷ 4.9) = 0.44 s. At 24 frames a second that is 10 frames; the ball should touch the water on frame 11. Watch the counter in Step 25. The widget below lets you change the height and the mass.

    Free fall

    Drop height and mass. One of these changes the clock; the other does not.

  2. Gravity for the ball

    Properties editor › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column)

    Do this:

    1. a
      Ball selected. Physics tab › Rigid Body (the Dynamic Paint button already shows an ×; both stay on). Type Active.
    2. b
      Mass 2. Collisions › Shape Sphere.
    3. c
      Open Surface Response: Bounciness 0.3.

    You should now see: a Rigid Body panel reading Active, 2 kg, Sphere, Bounciness 0.3.

    Why Sphere, and why 2 kg?

    The collision shape is what the physics engine sees. Sphere is exact for a ball and the fastest shape there is. Mesh (the Word lab’s choice) is slow and only needed for shapes with holes, like the cup. Mass does not change how fast the ball falls, only how hard it hits: try 20 kg in the widget above and count the frames.

  3. A cup that catches

    Properties editor › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column)

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Cup. Physics tab › Rigid Body. Type Passive: it stops the ball but never moves itself.
    2. b
      Collisions › Shape Mesh. A box or a hull would seal the top; Mesh keeps the hole.
    3. c
      Source Final, so the collision shape includes the Solidify wall. The Water gets no Rigid Body at all.

    You should now see: a Rigid Body panel on the Cup reading Passive, Mesh, Final.

    Why no Rigid Body on the water?

    A rigid body is solid. If the water were one, the ball would bounce off its surface like a floor. Leaving it out lets the ball pass through to the glass bottom; the Dynamic Paint brush, not physics, is what makes the splash. (Real buoyancy would need a fluid simulation: Blender’s Mantaflow. That is another lab.)

  4. Drop it

    The viewport and the Timeline along the bottom of the window.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Shift+←: frame 1. Mouse over the viewport, Space.
    2. b
      Watch the frame counter: the ball falls for ten frames and touches the water on frame 11. Rings race out from where it went in.
    3. c
      It sinks, settles on the glass floor by about frame 16 and rolls to a stop. The rings bounce off the glass and fade. Space to pause.

    You should now see: a drop, a splash of rings, a ball resting on the bottom of the glass with the water still sloshing. Not matching? See the ball falls through the cup or no splash.

    Is the first play the simulation?

    Yes. Blender works the physics out frame by frame the first time it plays and caches the result; after that it just replays. Change the mass or the height and the cache is thrown away: it recomputes on the next play. Step 26 locks it in.

  5. Bake the drop

    Properties editor › the cone-and-ball Scene tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Cache: End 120.
    2. b
      Click Bake. A progress bar runs; the button becomes Delete Bake.
    3. c
      Scrub anywhere in the timeline: the ball is always right. (The ripples are not baked; they recompute while you play, which is fine.)

    You should now see: the Cache panel showing Delete Bake, and the ball’s drop the same every time.

    Why bake?

    Rendering jumps straight to each frame instead of playing from 1, and an unbaked rigid body can only be computed in order. Baked, every frame is stored, so the render and the scrub are trustworthy. Changed something? Delete Bake, play once, Bake again.

End of Part 4. Save. Count the frames from 1 to the splash on your own screen and compare with the 10 the physics predicted.

Part 5

Light, camera, render

Tools: the Light, World and Camera tabs, Add › Light › Area, Cycles for a still, EEVEE for the movie.

Glass is nothing without something to reflect. A pale sky, a sun for fill, one big soft key light for the highlight on the ball and the sparkle on the rim; then a camera placed by number, a Cycles still of the splash and a five-second EEVEE movie.

  1. A sun and a sky

    The Outliner, the green bulb Data tab, the N sidebar › Item tab and the red globe World tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Outliner › click Light. Data tab: click Sun. Strength 2.
    2. b
      Sidebar: Rotation X 50, Y 10, Z -60. Sunlight from the front-left, over your shoulder.
    3. c
      World tab › Color › Hex B8C6D4: a pale sky.

    You should now see: in Rendered view the background turns pale grey-blue and the glass starts to shine: it is reflecting the sky.

    Why does the sky matter so much?

    Glass and water are mostly reflection and refraction: what you see in them is their surroundings. A black world gives a black, dead glass. A pale world fills it with light. This is why renders of glass always have something around them.

  2. A big soft key light

    Add › Light › Area, then the N sidebar › Item tab and the green bulb Data tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Light › Area. Sidebar: Location X 1.6, Y -1.8, Z 2.6.
    2. b
      Rotation X 53, Y 0, Z 42: it points at the cup.
    3. c
      Data tab: Power 500 W, Size 2. F2: Key.

    You should now see: a bright highlight on the ball and a sparkle on the rim of the glass; soft shadows on the table.

    Why so big?

    A 2 m light panel makes soft-edged shadows and a wide, gentle highlight, like a window. A small bright point makes a pin-prick glint and hard shadows. Photographers call this the key light: the one the picture is built around. The sun is the fill.

  3. The camera

    The Outliner, the N sidebar › Item tab, and the green camera Data tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Outliner › Camera. Sidebar: Location X 2.6, Y -3.3, Z 1.9.
    2. b
      Rotation X 78, Y 0, Z 38. Data tab: Focal Length 40.
    3. c
      Numpad 0: through the camera. The cup, the water, the ball above it, the table across the bottom.

    You should now see: the camera view with the cup a little below centre and empty sky above, room for the ball at frame 1. Not matching? See Numpad 0 shows nothing useful.

    Why so much sky?

    At frame 1 the ball is at Z 2, a metre above the rim. A tighter frame would cut it off for the first ten frames. 40 mm is a slightly wide lens; 50 mm (the default) would need the camera further back.

  4. A still of the splash (Cycles)

    The Render tab, then the render window and its Image menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Frame box: 12, the moment the ball touches the water. Render tab › Render Engine Cycles. Sampling › Render › Max Samples 64, Denoise ticked.
    2. b
      F12. Cycles traces the light through the glass and the water: one to three minutes.
    3. c
      In the render window: Image › Save As › PNG. Name it Lab21_BallInACup_YourName_render. Save it next to your .blend.

    You should now see: a photo of the splash: the ball breaking the water line, the rim of the glass catching the key light, the wood grain under it. Checkpoint E below.

    Why Cycles for the still?

    Cycles traces real light paths: it can follow a ray through the glass, into the water, off the ball and back out. EEVEE fakes it quickly and well enough for a movie, but the still is where every bounce shows.

  5. The movie (EEVEE)

    The Render tab, the Output tab, then the Render menu in the top bar.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Render tab › Render Engine back to EEVEE (Raytracing is still ticked from Step 21). Output tab › Resolution 50%.
    2. b
      Output panel: Media Type Video. Encoding › Container MPEG-4. The folder box: your Lab 21 folder.
    3. c
      Render › Render Animation (or Ctrl+F12). 120 frames: a few minutes. Then Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: a file called 0001-0120.mp4 in your folder: five seconds of sloshing water, a drop, a splash, rings. Checkpoint F below.

    Why 50%?

    120 frames at full size with raytracing is a long wait on a school machine. Half size is a quarter of the pixels and looks fine on a screen. Set it back to 100% at home if you want.

  6. Save and hand in

    The File menu and SEQTA.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Ctrl+S. The title bar loses its asterisk.
    2. b
      Upload three files to SEQTA — Lab 21: Lab21_BallInACup_YourName.blend, Lab21_BallInACup_YourName_render.png and the 0001-0120.mp4.
    3. c
      Not finished? Upload what you have and say which step you reached.

    You should now see: three files in SEQTA, and a save with no asterisk.

End of the lab. Save, upload, and then try an extension.

Part 6

Finished early? Pick one

Tools: everything above, used again.

Each one is a small project on its own. They are written as moves, not steps: you know the tools now.

A second ball

Click the Ball, Shift+D, then type X -0.2 and Enter (a copy, 20 cm to the left). Sidebar: Z 2.6 so it lands later. It already has the Rigid Body and the brush: Shift+D copies both. Scene tab › Delete Bake, play, Bake. Two splashes, two sets of rings crossing each other. F2 it Ball.002, or give it a new material: Hex 2A7BD5.

Closer

The checkpoint F picture used a second camera. Add › Camera, Location 1.9, -2.4, 1.45, Rotation 74, 0, 38, Focal Length 50. Scene tab › Camera: pick it. Numpad 0. Render frame 13. Or keyframe the original camera instead: at frame 1 press I over the viewport with the camera selected (Location and Rotation), go to frame 120, type the closer numbers, I again. The shot pushes in as the ball drops, the Word lab’s “movie scene”.

A bouncier ball, a heavier ball

Bounciness 0.9: Delete Bake, play. It bounces off the glass floor and back out of the water. Mass 20: same ten frames to fall (count them), but the Clamp of 0.06 keeps the splash the same size too. Raise the brush Clamp to 0.15 and the heavy ball’s splash grows. Which setting really made the difference? Write it down.

Rougher sea, calmer sea

OceanPlane › Ocean › Waves › Scale 0.1: the slosh climbs the glass. Choppiness 3: peaks. Scale 0.01: a glass left on a table, barely moving. Try Time keys of 1 and 12 instead of 1 and 6: twice as fast. Watch the Shrinkwrap Limit: with Scale 0.1 the waves are 10 cm tall and the Limit of 0.3 still covers them; at 0.4 it would not.

Colour the water

Material Water: Base Color Hex E8C55A and Transmission Weight 0.9 for apple juice; Hex 5A2A0E, Roughness 0.05, Transmission 0.6 for cola. Add Volume › Volume Absorption (in the node editor: Shift+A › Shader › Volume Absorption, wired to the Material Output’s Volume socket) with Density 8 and the colour deepens with depth, as real drinks do.

Slow motion

Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Speed 0.25, and Water › Dynamic Paint › Waves › Speed 0.25. Timeline End 240. Delete Bake, Bake. The drop takes 40 frames and the splash unfolds; render the movie again. (The ocean slosh keeps its own clock: key Time 1 and 3 instead of 1 and 6 so it slows too.)

Something’s not right

Find the problem that matches yours.

F2 only shows a box for a name; I can’t find Cup (or Water, OceanPlane, Ball, Key…)

That box is the whole point. F2 is Rename: the box is where you type the object’s new name, then Enter. Cup, Water, OceanPlane, Ball and Key are names this lab gives to things you have just made; they are not tools. If a step says “F2: Water”, it means: press F2, type Water, press Enter. (F3 is a different key, Search; close it with Esc if you opened it.)

The Add Cylinder (or Add UV Sphere) panel vanished before I changed the numbers

It closes on your next click anywhere else. Delete the object (X) and add it again; set every number in the panel before touching anything else. If the panel is folded, click its title bottom-left to open it. You can also fix it afterwards in the sidebar (N): Location Z, and Scale for the radius; but Vertices can only be set in the panel.

The lid is still there, or the whole cylinder vanished

In Edit Mode with face mode (3), click only the top face, then X › Faces. If everything disappeared you had all faces selected: Ctrl+Z, click empty space to deselect, click the lid alone. If the lid came back, you pressed Tab before deleting: Tab again and look.

Solidify made the glass fatter on the outside

Offset is 1 instead of -1. In the Solidify panel set Offset to -1: the wall grows inward and the outside stays at radius 0.5. (The Water’s radius of 0.45 was chosen for an inside of 0.46.)

Grid Fill did nothing, or filled the wrong thing

Grid Fill needs the rim of edges selected and nothing else. Edge mode (2), click empty space to deselect, then Alt+click one rim edge: the status bar (bottom right) should say 48 edges. If the lid is still there you deleted with X › Faces instead of Only Faces (Step 10): Ctrl+Z and redo. If the fill is a mess of triangles, you used Face › Fill or F: Ctrl+Z and pick Grid Fill from the Face menu.

The water (or the plane) does not move when I scrub

Three usual causes. The Ocean’s Time is not keyed: hover the Time box on frame 1, type 1, press I; frame 120, type 6, press I; the box should be yellow on those frames and green between (Step 13). The Shrinkwrap has no Target: pick OceanPlane. The Shrinkwrap is on the OceanPlane instead of the Water: remove it (the X in its header), click the Water, add it there.

The whole water cylinder jumped onto the plane and went flat

The Shrinkwrap’s Limit is 0. Set Limit 0.3 so only vertices within 0.3 m of the plane move: the top grid is 0 m away, the bottom ring 0.86 m. Also check Wrap Method is Project with Axis Z; Nearest Surface Point drags the walls sideways.

Blender is slow since Part 2

Resolution 10 and three Simple subdivision levels is 12 000 faces of water moving every frame, plus the ocean. Set the Water’s Subdivision Levels Viewport to 2 while you work (Render stays 3), and the Ocean’s Resolution Viewport to 7. Pause the film when you are not watching it. Save: Ctrl+S.

The ball makes no ripples

Almost always the dropdown. Click the Ball, Physics tab: the Dynamic Paint panel must say Brush with a Remove Brush button. If it says Canvas with Remove Canvas, click Remove Canvas, change Type to Brush, click Add Brush (Step 19). Then: the Water must say Canvas with Surface Type Waves (Step 18). Ripples only compute while the film plays (Space), from frame 1: Shift+Left, then Space, then drag. And the ball must actually touch the water: it is at Z 0.9, half in.

Dragging while it plays is jerky, or the ball lags behind the mouse

Rendered view costs time. Z › Solid while you drag, Rendered to look. Or lower the Water’s Subdivision Viewport to 2 (see slow). Press G once, move, click once; holding the mouse button down while pressing G confuses it.

The cup is not see-through in Rendered view

Three checks. Render tab › Raytracing must be ticked (Step 21): without it EEVEE draws glass as a grey lump. The Glass material’s Transmission Weight must be 1 (Material tab, open the Transmission panel). And the viewport must be in Rendered shading, not Material Preview: Z › Rendered. Still dark? The World is black until Step 27; the glass is see-through but has nothing to show. Finish Part 5 and look again.

The ball falls straight through the cup and the table

The cup has no Rigid Body, or its shape is wrong. Click the Cup: Physics tab must show Rigid Body, Type Passive, Shape Mesh, Source Final (Step 24). Convex Hull or Box would seal the top instead (the ball bounces off a lid you cannot see). The table needs nothing: the ball never reaches it if the cup is right.

The ball falls in but there is no splash

The brush and the canvas from Part 3 are still needed in Part 4; if you removed either, redo Steps 18 and 19. Then play from frame 1 (Shift+Left, Space): Dynamic Paint only computes while the film plays forward. The splash also needs the brush Source to be Mesh Volume so the whole ball counts, not just its centre point.

The water explodes out of the cup when the ball hits

The brush Clamp is 0 (off). Ball › Dynamic Paint › Waves › Clamp 0.06: the biggest push the ball can give is 6 cm. A 2 kg ball at 4 m/s would otherwise push several metres of wave.

The ball bounces back out of the water

Bounciness is too high. Ball › Rigid Body › Surface Response › Bounciness 0.3 (Step 23). 0.9 is a superball. Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Delete Bake, play, Bake.

I changed the mass (or the height) and nothing changed

The drop is baked. Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Cache › Delete Bake, then play from frame 1, then Bake again. A baked simulation is frozen on purpose: that is what makes rendering safe.

The render is almost black

The World colour is still the default near-black (Step 27), or the lights are off. World tab › Color › Hex B8C6D4. Outliner: the Light and Key rows should have their camera icons on. Sun Strength 2, Key Power 500 W.

Numpad 0 shows nothing useful

Check the camera’s numbers in the sidebar: Location 2.6, -3.3, 1.9 and Rotation 78, 0, 38, lens 40 mm. If you typed into the wrong object, click Camera in the Outliner first. No numpad? Click the camera icon in the little column under the gizmo, or View › Cameras › Active Camera.

Render Animation makes pictures, not a movie

Media Type is still Image. Output tab › Output panel › Media Type › Video, Container MPEG-4, then render again. The movie lands in the folder shown in the output path box; by default that is a temporary folder, so set it to your Lab folder first.

The render has speckles in the glass

Cycles noise. Render tab › Sampling › Render: Denoise ticked, Max Samples 64 (128 if you have time). In EEVEE, Render tab › Raytracing › Denoising on. Speckles that crawl in the movie are the same thing: more samples or lower resolution.

I can’t orbit (no middle mouse button)

Drag on the coloured gizmo itself to orbit. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate 3 Button Mouse, then Alt + left-drag orbits.

I have no number pad (Numpad 0)

Use the camera icon in the column under the gizmo, or View › Cameras › Active Camera. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate Numpad; but then the 1, 2, 3 keys change the view instead of the select mode, so click the three select buttons in the header instead.

Ten quick questions

Pick an answer to lock it in. You’ll find out straight away whether you’re right.

1The Add Cylinder panel says Depth 1.2 and Location Z 0.6. Where is the bottom of the cylinder?

Right. The panel’s Location is the centre; 0.6 − 1.2 ÷ 2 = 0.

Not quite. Location is the centre of the cylinder, and half of 1.2 is 0.6, so the bottom lands at 0.6 − 0.6 = 0.

2Why does the water have a hidden plane under its surface?

Right. The plane is the engine, the cylinder is the body; Shrinkwrap joins them.

Not quite. Ocean needs a plane. The plane makes the waves; a Shrinkwrap on the water’s top grid copies them. It is hidden because it is not meant to be seen.

3The Shrinkwrap’s Limit is 0.3. What does it protect?

Right. Only vertices within 0.3 m move; the top grid is 0 m away, the bottom 0.86 m.

Not quite. Limit is a distance. Vertices further than 0.3 m from the plane are left alone, which keeps the water’s bottom and walls where they are.

4A step says “F2: OceanPlane”. What do you do?

Right. F2 is Rename: OceanPlane is the name you give the plane you just added.

Not quite. F2 opens the Rename Active Item box; OceanPlane is a name you type into it, not a tool. F3 is Search, a different key.

5The Ocean modifier is on and the plane does not move when you scrub. Most likely?

Right. Time is the clock; a key at each end of the timeline makes it run.

Not quite. The Ocean modifier is a photo of one moment until its Time is animated: key 1 on frame 1 and 6 on frame 120.

6Dynamic Paint: which is the canvas and which is the brush?

Right. The canvas is marked; the brush marks it. The dropdown opens on Canvas every time, so the ball’s must be changed.

Not quite. The water gets the marks (canvas); the ball makes them (brush). That dropdown is the one everyone gets wrong once.

7The ball is 0.93 m above the water. How many frames until it touches, at 24 fps?

Right. t = √(2 × 0.93 ÷ 9.81) = 0.44 s; 0.44 × 24 ≈ 10 frames. Mass does not come into it.

Not quite. Height = 4.9 t², so t = √(0.93 ÷ 4.9) = 0.44 s, which is about 10 frames. Mass changes the hit, not the clock.

8Why does the cup get Shape Mesh but the ball gets Shape Sphere?

Right. Convex Hull or Box would seal the cup’s opening and the ball would bounce off a lid you cannot see.

Not quite. The collision shape is what the physics sees. Sphere is perfect for a ball. The cup needs Mesh so its opening stays open; a hull would stretch a skin over it.

9Why does the water get no Rigid Body?

Right. The splash is Dynamic Paint, not physics; the ball must pass through to the glass floor.

Not quite. Rigid bodies are solid. The ball needs to go through the water, so the water stays out of the physics and the brush makes the splash.

10Glass has IOR 1.45 and water 1.33. What does that give you in the render?

Right. Two surfaces, two bends: the break at the water line is what reads as “wet”.

Not quite. IOR is how much light bends going in. Two different IORs means two different bends, so straight things look broken at the water line.

Check yourself

Tick each one you can honestly do now. Anything left unticked is what to ask about next lesson.

Think about it

Lift the ball to Z 3 instead of 2. How many frames to the water now, and what else would you need to change so the camera still sees it at frame 1? And: the ripples are computed by a canvas and a brush, the drop by a rigid body, the slosh by an Ocean modifier. Which of the three is “real physics”, and does it matter for the picture?

Upload to SEQTA — Lab 21

Upload Lab21_BallInACup_YourName.blend, your Cycles still Lab21_BallInACup_YourName_render.png and your movie 0001-0120.mp4 (rename it Lab21_BallInACup_YourName.mp4 if you like). The .blend should contain a Cup with Solidify, Bevel and Subdivision and a Passive Mesh rigid body; a Water with Shrinkwrap, Subdivision and a Dynamic Paint canvas; a hidden OceanPlane with keyed Time; a Ball with a brush and an Active rigid body, baked; Table, Light, Key and Camera placed by number.

Due one week from when this lab was handed out.

Teacher notes

Timing

Three lessons. Lesson 1: Parts 1–2 (the glass, the table, the water that sloshes). Lesson 2: Parts 3–4 (Dynamic Paint, ripples by hand, the gravity drop and the bake). Lesson 3: Part 5 (light, camera, Cycles still, EEVEE movie) and extensions. The 120-frame EEVEE render at 50% with raytracing takes 3–8 minutes on a school machine; start it before packing up. The Cycles still at 64 samples takes one to three minutes.

What this lab is

One lab made from two Word labs, Lab 10 Water Splashing Motion (a cylinder of water whose Grid-Filled top shrinkwraps onto a hidden plane with an Ocean modifier) and Lab 11 Object in the Ocean (Dynamic Paint: a canvas with Surface Type Waves and a sphere as a brush), with the Rigid Body drop from Lab 9A Gravity and movement added so the ball falls in. The two water tricks are kept exactly as the originals had them; everything else (a real glass with a wall, a wooden table, materials with the right IORs, a sky, a key light, a camera by number, a bake, a still and a movie) is added so the result looks like a photograph and a Year 9 student can get there without a YouTube link. It is numbered Lab 21 because the HTML series already has a Lab 11 (the Car); the Word files’ own numbers are 10 and 11.

Audit of the source labs

Lab 10 (Word). Correctness: “Pane” for Plane throughout; “Shift+G+Z” for move-on-Z (it is G then Z); step 3 says to move the cylinder up so the plane is at its bottom, step 4 to move the plane to its top (contradictory; the plane belongs at the water line); the Ocean settings are a screenshot (Repeat 1, Resolution 14, Time 15, Depth 200, Size 1, Spatial Size 14): Resolution 14 gives a 196 × 196 grid, and the later Subdivision 3 on the cylinder multiplies the shrinkwrapped faces by 64, heavy for school machines; the Shrinkwrap is set to Project with no axis, direction or limit, so as written the whole cylinder (bottom included) can project onto the plane; “Insert keyframes at 0 and 70 (similar to the last lab)” never says what is keyed (the Ocean’s Time), and frame 0 is outside the default range; “change the lighting colour and then render it” is the only lighting or camera instruction. Completeness: no material, no camera, no output settings, no mention that the Time slider must be animated for the movie. Clarity: step numbers run 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; several steps are sentence fragments under a screenshot; the second cylinder’s modifier stack is only a screenshot (Bevel 0.1, Solidify 0.059 offset −1, Subdivision). Pedagogy: no explanation of why the plane exists or what Shrinkwrap does, so students copy without a model to reason from. The file name “Lab 10.blend” has a space.

Lab 11 (Word). Correctness: “Press play to preview” (step 5) shows a frozen ocean, because the Ocean modifier’s Time is never keyed or driven in this lab; “Delete all objects” removes the camera and it is never added back, so the file cannot be rendered as written; “Click on the ball and drag it around” (step 12) only makes ripples while the timeline is playing, which is not said; step 11 “Click on Dynamic paint again and select Brush, then add brush” does not say it is on the ball, and the panel opens on Canvas, which is the single most common failure (this lab draws the dropdown in Step 19 and gives it a fix and a quiz question). Completeness: no render, no output settings, lighting is “add some light”; the ball material is a screenshot; the realism (“The ocean looks terrible”) and the camera animation are outsourced to two YouTube videos, one marked intermediate. Clarity: “settinsg”, “shere”, “pane”; the Ocean values 0.35 and 2.59 are arbitrary precision with no reason given. Suitability: the only part a Year 9 can finish from the page is a grey sphere on a grey, frozen plane.

Lab 9A (Word), used for the drop: Shape Mesh on a small cube where Box is exact and fast; Mass 20 kg and damping 0.314 / 0.608 with no reason; “Render your file” without any camera or output step; Section B is only a video link; duplicate step numbers. This lab uses Sphere for the ball, Mesh only where the hole needs it (the cup), and explains every number.

Design decisions

  • Ripples by hand come before the drop (Part 3 before Part 4). A rigid body cannot be dragged while it is simulating, so the Word lab’s click-and-drag ripples and the gravity drop are taught as two separate tricks on the same ball. Part 3 has the ball on the surface; Part 4 lifts it. Students who want to drag after the drop remove the ball’s Rigid Body (Physics tab, the × on its button) and play.
  • The water gets no Rigid Body. A rigid body is solid; the ball would bounce off the surface. The splash is the Dynamic Paint brush entering the canvas. Real buoyancy would need Mantaflow; Step 24’s Why says so.
  • Clamp 0.06 on the brush stops the falling ball from throwing the water out of the cup (the fix the water explodes). Damping 0.05 makes the rings fade in about two seconds.
  • Shrinkwrap with Limit 0.3, Project along Z in both directions, so only the Grid-Filled top moves. This is the setting the Word lab leaves out.
  • Ocean on a hidden 1.2 m plane at the water line (Spatial Size 3, Wave Scale 0.04, Choppiness 1.5, Time keyed 1 → 6 over 120 frames): cup-sized waves, 4 cm high. The OceanPlane is hidden in viewport and render but still drives the Shrinkwrap.
  • Simple subdivision on the water (not Catmull-Clark) so the rim is not rounded away from the glass. Three levels: 12 000 faces of surface.
  • Glass 1.45, water 1.33, both Transmission 1, under a pale World (B8C6D4), a sun and a 2 m area key: the two IORs and the reflected sky are what make the render read as wet. The refraction widget under Step 16 is there to make IOR a number students can see.
  • Three widgets: refraction (Snell’s law, draggable IOR), a ripple tank (the same height-field wave equation Dynamic Paint Waves solves, with the lab’s Damping slider), and free fall (height and mass sliders; only one changes the frame count). Each sits next to the step it explains.

Tested values

Every number, menu path and shortcut was checked by building the scene from these steps in Blender 5.2 (bpy): the ball enters the water at frame 12 (predicted 11; the first frame is 1 and the drop starts at rest), settles at Z 0.18 by frame 18, the surface follows the ocean within ±3 cm, the drag ripples are 8–13 cm tall. The checkpoint pictures, the hero still and the filmstrip were rendered from that file (Cycles, 32–48 samples). Blender 4.2 or newer: Raytracing in EEVEE (Step 21) arrived in 4.2; the Media Type › Video output setting in Step 31 is Blender 4.5+ (on 4.2 it is File Format › FFmpeg Video). The finished .blend is supplied with this lab.

Where students usually get stuck

The Dynamic Paint Type dropdown left on Canvas for the ball (Step 19). Dragging the ball while the film is paused (Step 20). Deleting the water’s lid with Faces instead of Only Faces, so there is no rim for Grid Fill (Step 10). Shrinkwrap on the wrong object, or Limit 0 (Step 14). Forgetting to key Time, so nothing moves (Step 13). The Add Cylinder panel closing early (Steps 2, 9, 17). Raytracing off, so the glass is a grey lump in Rendered view (Step 21). Cup shape Convex Hull, so the ball bounces off an invisible lid (Step 24). Changing the mass without Delete Bake (Step 26). Output still on Image, so the movie is 120 PNGs (Step 31).

Quiz answers

1 On the grid, 0 m. 2 Ocean needs a plane; Shrinkwrap copies it. 3 The bottom of the water. 4 Press F2, type it, Enter. 5 Time has no keys. 6 Water canvas, ball brush. 7 About 10. 8 Sphere is exact; the cup’s hole needs Mesh. 9 It would be solid. 10 The outline breaks at the water line.

Quick rubric
